issues.subcategory: unsupported extrapolation to untested population
issues.description: The study used exclusively sex-segregated (single-sex) chains, as stated in the Methods ('exclusively males or exclusively females'). The manuscript nonetheless asserts that the findings generalize to mixed-gender settings. No mixed-gender condition was run, so this claim is entirely unsupported by the data and directly contradicts the design. It is a clear generalizability overclaim.
issues.quote: These findings generalize beyond the single-sex chain compositions used here, suggesting cultural transmission operates similarly in mixed-gender collaborative settings.

issues.subcategory: non-randomized treatment driving causal claims
issues.description: The type of theory a participant inherited (inertia, centre-of-mass, full, or irrelevant) was not experimentally assigned; it emerged from the prior participant's behavior within the chain. Participants who inherited an inertia theory therefore differ systematically from those who inherited a centre-of-mass theory (e.g., their predecessors discovered different parameters), confounding any inference. Strong causal language ('strongly affected', 'prevented them from noticing') is applied to what is essentially an observational subgroup comparison.
issues.quote: Furthermore, inherited theories strongly affected participant's understanding of the wheel system.

issues.subcategory: underpowered subgroups
issues.description: Key exploratory conclusions about theory effects rest on extremely small subgroups created by post-hoc coding (15, 17, 6, and 18 participants), with the 'full theory' group containing only 6 individuals. Conclusions drawn from such small, non-randomly-formed subgroups are statistically fragile and were not powered for.
issues.quote: The few participants who inherited a full theory (N = 6) produced compact and asymmetrical wheels (D-H).

issues.subcategory: confirming a null without power analysis or equivalence testing
issues.description: The central claims (understanding does not improve; theory transmission has no effect on optimization/understanding) are affirmations of null results based on credible intervals that include zero and are very wide (e.g., treatment CI -10.76 to 18.13). With only 5 generations and no power analysis or equivalence/ROPE test, absence of evidence is being interpreted as evidence of absence. The design favours the predicted null simply through low power.
issues.quote: Thus, these analyses do not provide substantial support for the idea that the transmission of explicit causal theories affects wheel optimization and individual understanding.

issues.subcategory: post-hoc model selection in a preregistered analysis
issues.description: Analysis 1 is labeled as a preregistered analysis, yet the final model was chosen after comparing multiple candidate models on their fit to the observed data. Selecting model specification based on fit to the data introduces undisclosed researcher degrees of freedom and undermines the preregistration. The candidate set, selection criterion, and how this departs from the registered plan are not specified.
issues.quote: The final model specification was selected after comparing several candidate models based on fit to the observed data.

issues.subcategory: contradictory statements about data exclusion
issues.description: The Methods state that no data points were excluded, but speed analyses were restricted to participants' last two trials (excluding trials 1-3) and the reported speeds are averages over 'non-failure wheels' only (excluding wheels that did not descend). These exclusions directly contradict the claim that no data points were excluded and could bias speed estimates upward.
issues.quote: No data points were excluded from the analyses.

issues.subcategory: missing prior specifications for Bayesian models
issues.description: All inferences derive from Bayesian multilevel models, but no prior distributions are reported for any model. Without the priors (and other sampling details such as chains, iterations, convergence diagnostics), the Bayesian credible intervals cannot be reproduced or evaluated, which is critical given that conclusions hinge on whether intervals include zero.
issues.quote: We ran a series of Bayesian multi-level models in R 32.  Models were fitted using map2stan in the rethinking package 33 and 95% credible intervals were used to make inferences.

issues.subcategory: wrong agreement statistic for three raters
issues.description: Cohen's kappa is defined for two raters, but three raters coded the theories. Inter-rater agreement among three raters should be assessed with Fleiss' kappa (or an averaged pairwise approach). It is also unclear how disagreements among the three coders were resolved to produce the final codes.
issues.quote: Cohen’s kappa coefficients reveal almost perfect agreement between raters (0.81 for inertia and 0.85 for centre of mass).

issues.subcategory: inconsistent measurement distance for speed
issues.description: Speed is defined and computed as 1 m divided by descent time, and the track is described as 1 meter long, but the timing switches were placed 92 cm apart. If timing occurred over 92 cm, computing speed as 1 m / time systematically misstates the actual speeds. The distance used in the speed calculation is internally inconsistent and not reconciled.
issues.quote: Two push-button switches (made from computer mice) were located 92 cm apart on the rails

issues.subcategory: inconsistent generation counting and optimization denominator
issues.description: The text states wheel speed increased 'After 5 generations' but then reports 'optimization of 71% after only four cultural generations.' Furthermore, the basis of the 71% figure is unclear: (145.7-123.6)/(154-123.6) = ~73%, not 71%, and the chosen baseline/denominator is not defined. The generation count and the optimization percentage are both ambiguous/inconsistent.
issues.quote: Given that the maximum possible speed was about 154 m/h, these results indicate an optimization of 71% after only four cultural generations.

issues.subcategory: credible interaction dismissed
issues.description: The Generation x Treatment interaction for understanding has a 95% credible interval (0.03, 0.81) that excludes zero, which by the authors' own inferential criterion (using 95% credible intervals to make inferences) indicates a credible effect. Yet this is verbally minimized as 'slightly better' and the section concludes there is no substantial support for theory transmission affecting understanding. The interpretation is inconsistent with the reported statistics.
issues.quote: although participants in the very last generation had a slightly better understanding when they had inherited a theory (Treatment 95% CI: (-2.54, 0.31), mean = -1.14; Generation x Treatment 95% CI: (0.03, 0.81), mean = 0.44, Figure 2.B)

issues.subcategory: prediction accuracy equated with causal understanding
issues.description: The 10 paired forced-choice predictions measure whether participants can predict which wheel is faster along a single isolated dimension. This is operationalized as 'causal understanding,' but predictive accuracy on isolated comparisons is not the same construct as causal/mechanistic understanding, and the test never requires integrating the two dimensions as the optimization task does. The strong claim of 'rigorously' measuring causal understanding overstates what the measure captures.
issues.quote: This allowed us to rigorously measure participants’ causal understanding of the system after they completed their 5 trials (Figure 1.E).

issues.subcategory: absence of blinding and experimenter involvement
issues.description: The experimenter manually positioned the weights and released the wheel on each trial, and data collection was not blind to condition. Manual positioning/release introduces a potential source of measurement variability and experimenter bias in performance outcomes, and the lack of blinding is acknowledged but its potential effects are not addressed.
issues.quote: Data collection and was not performed blind to the conditions of the experiments.

issues.subcategory: handling of non-descending (failed) wheels unspecified
issues.description: Wheels that did not descend ('failures') cannot yield a finite speed (1/time), so they must be excluded or otherwise handled in the speed models, yet the procedure for incorporating or excluding these failures into the Bayesian models is not described. Failures are informative about poor configurations, and excluding them biases speed estimates and obscures exploration costs. This also conflicts with the 'no data excluded' claim.
issues.quote: Vertical bars show the number of wheels that did not descend (i.e. failures) at each trial in each treatment. Coloured lines show the average speed for non-failure wheels at each trial in each treatment.

issues.subcategory: post-hoc aggregation masking key dimension
issues.description: The preregistered analysis 4 modeled understanding separately by physical principle, but because it did not converge, the authors aggregated scores and removed the Physical Principle terms. Aggregating eliminates exactly the inertia-vs-centre-of-mass contrast that is central to the paper's exploratory conclusions, and the non-convergence/deviation creates flexibility in what is reported. Although disclosed, the consequences for inference are not fully evaluated.
issues.quote: As a result, the preregistered model did not converge so we ran our analysis on aggregated score and removed the terms associated the variable “Physical Principle” in the reported model.

issues.subcategory: comparison group omits eligible no-theory participants
issues.description: The 'did not inherit any theory' comparison group is reported as N=70 (the Configurations treatment), but the 14 first-generation participants in the Configurations+Theory treatment also inherited no theory and are excluded from this group. This selective grouping is not justified and could bias the theory-vs-no-theory understanding comparison.
issues.quote: Participants who did not inherit any theory (N = 70) sampled various positions along each spoke (A)

issues.subcategory: overstated 'absence of understanding' given above-chance baseline
issues.description: The headline framing ('in the absence of explicit causal understanding') is overstated: first-generation participants already scored above chance (4.60 vs ~3.33), and the Discussion concedes participants had 'appropriate intuitions about how to maximize acceleration' that 'accelerated cultural evolution.' Thus participants possessed and used partial causal understanding/intuitions; the accurate claim is that understanding did not increase, not that it was absent.
issues.quote: Here, we show that a physical artifact becomes progressively optimized across generations of social learners in the absence of explicit causal understanding.

issues.subcategory: extrapolation from lab wheel to complex real technology and archaeology
issues.description: Conclusions are extended to real-world complex technologies (bows, kayaks) and to interpreting 'complex archaeological materials,' based on a 2-dimensional lab wheel task with WEIRD university students. The authors note the low dimensionality is 'conservative,' but a 2-D problem may actually be easier to understand than high-D technologies, so the direction of the bias is arguable and the leap to archaeological inference is large and insufficiently caveated.
issues.quote: our experiment indicates that one should be cautious when interpreting complex archaeological materials as evidence for sophisticated cognitive abilities (such as reasoning, problem-solving or planning), since these abilities are not the sole driver of technological sophistication

issues.subcategory: circular/post-hoc grouping in mechanism test
issues.description: The mechanism test (Supplementary Figure 2) groups Configurations participants by the type of wheels they produced (balanced/unbalanced/various) and then relates this to their understanding scores. Because exploration behavior and understanding are both outcomes that may share common causes, grouping on one outcome to explain another is post-hoc and potentially circular, not a clean test of the causal mechanism.
issues.quote: we grouped participants who did not inherit any theory (i.e. from the “Configurations” treatment) into 3 categories: those who produced various types of wheels, those who only produced balanced wheels, and those who only produced unbalanced wheels.

issues.subcategory: weak incentive for understanding test undisclosed in interpretation
issues.description: Only one of the ten test answers, selected at random, was incentivized (5€). This is a weak and noisy incentive for accuracy on the understanding measure, which is central to the null finding about understanding. The potential for low motivation/measurement noise to depress and flatten understanding scores across generations is not discussed.
issues.quote: They were also told that one of their answers will be randomly selected at the end of the test and that 5 euros will be added to their gain if that answer is correct.

issues.subcategory: inconsistent maximum-speed constants
issues.description: The payoff function uses MaxSpeed = 160, but the Results state the maximum possible speed was 'about 154 m/h.' These two reference values are not reconciled, and since the 71% optimization figure depends on the maximum, the discrepancy affects interpretation of how close to optimal participants got.
issues.quote: with MaxSpeed  = 160, MinSpeed = 96.

issues.subcategory: random effect with minimal within-group data
issues.description: Speed analyses restricted to the last two trials include 'Player's identity' as a random effect, but each player then contributes only two observations, making the player-level variance component nearly confounded with residual error and potentially unstable. The adequacy and estimation of this random effect is not discussed.
issues.quote: We fitted a linear model with “Speed” as the outcome variable, “Trial”, “Generation” as predictor variables and “Player’s identity” and “Chain’s identity” as random effects
